ORAL ANSWERS TO QUESTIONS 
Pulse Polio Programme 
*521.  SHRIMATIJAMANA DEVI BARUPAL.†  
     DR. T. SUBBARAMIREDDY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to 
state: 
(a) whether International donor agencies have given India an additional 
Rs. 100 crore to help step up its Pulse Polio Programme and reach the target of 
polio eradication by 2005; 
(b) if so, to what extent eradication of polio has been successful in the 
country; 
(c) whether Government have chalked out any programme of eradication 
of polio in endemic States such as Uttar Pradesh and Bihar, 
(d) if so, the other States where the polio cases are on the increase and to 
what extent they have been controlled; and 
(e) whether Government are confident of eradicating polio from the 
country by 2005? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) to (e) A Stat ement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
The polio eradication activity is a Centrally Sponsored Scheme of the 
Government, for which donor assistance is mobilized either in cash or kind. 
The cash contributions are routed throu gh the Budget of the Department of 
Family Welfare, whereas that received in kind, mainly oral polio vaccine through 
UNICEF, is accounted for as receipt of commodities

Dev Barupal.

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
The vaccine supply for th e polio campaign is arranged Centrally, mainly 
through UNICEF, while for the operational expenses, grants are released to the 
States. 
During 2002-03, an expenditure of Rs. 483.18 crore was estimated, all of 
which was fully met from donor assistance. During 2003-04, an expense of Rs. 
656.54 crore has been estimated, out of which Rs. 311.99 crore will be spent on 
procurement of vaccine while Rs. 344. 55 crore will be spent on operational 
expenses. Against this, assistance from the existing Projects of World Bank, 
Department for International Development, United Kingdom. German 
Government, Centre for Diseases Control, United States of America and 
UNICEF is Rs. 322.8 crore. 
Over and above the aforementioned existing commitments of various 
multilatf ral and bilateral donor agencies, following commitments have been 
received or are likely from the Agencies listed in the Table below for the polio 
operations during the current year—

Polio eradication activities have been largely successful in reduction in 
number of polio cases from 1934 in 1998 to 268 in 2001. However, the polio 
eradication efforts suffered a major setback during 2002 due to large-scale 
outbreak in Uttar Pradesh and spill over transmission into other neighbouring 
States namely, Delhi, Haryana, Madhya Pradesh, Jharkhand, Uttaranchal. 
Gujarat, West Bengal and Rajasthan. The number of cases detected during the 
years 2001 and 2002 is annexed as Statement-I (See below). 
Following special measures have been taken with a special reference 
2 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
to the States of Uttar Pradesh, Bihar and other States where large number of polio 
cases have been detected: 
(i) In order to improve the detection and vaccination of missed children, 
the house-to-house vaccination teams have been strengthened with 
the addition of a third member preferably being a woman from within 
the local community. 
(ii) Community mobilizers have been engaged for improving the 
implementation of the programme in resistant areas. 
(iii) House-to-house vaccination of missed children in Bihar and Uttar 
Pradesh is being done for five days after the booth day as against two 
days in the other parts of the country. 
(iv) Additional IEC activities are being conducted by increasing mass 
media and interpersonal communication. 
(v) The implementation of the programme is being closely monitored at the 
apex political and bureaucratic levels both in the Government of 
India as also in the States. 
(vi) Local influencers/social and religious leaders are being involved for 
advocacy and ensuring greater part icipation of the people in the 
programme. 
Chief Ministers of the States of Bihar, Uttar Pradesh, Madhya Pradesh and 
Rajasthan have been addressed by the Prime Minister in a meeting to improve 
the quality of the implementation of the programme and to take all possible 
measures to stem the circulation of polio virus within their States. The State 
Governments have also taken a number of steps in order to improve the 
implementation of the programme and to ensure greater participation of the 
people. 
Increase in polio cases have also been observed in the States of West 
Bengal, Gujarat, Rajasthan, Jharkhand, Delhi and Haryana. These States are 
under special focus to improve the quality of immunization activities. One 
additional round of Pulse Polio Immunization has already been held on the 6th 
of April, 2003 and 3 additional rounds are being planned in 2003 in addition to 
two Nation-wide rounds being proposed in January and February, 2004. 
During, 2003 the number of polio cases detected so far has been 70. Most of 
the cases have been reported from the States of Uttar Pradesh, West Bengal, 
Bihar, Madhya Pradesh and Rajasthan. 
3 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
The polio eradication programme is implemented by the Government of 
India through States/UTs. The annual st rategies for achieving this goal are 
formulated and implemented by the Government on the basis of the advise of a 
group of National and International experts. National Immunization Days 
(NIDs) are conducted all over the country when all children below 5 years of 
age are given polio drops two times during the winter months. Besides this, 
Sub National Immunization Days (SNIDs) are also being conducted throughout 
the endemic areas where polio cases are reported to be increasing. 
The national goal is to eradicate polio from the country by 2005.

*531 .SHRI KHAN GHUFRAN ZAHIDI: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether It is a fact that the post of Drugs Controller General of India 
(DCGI) has not been regularised; and 
(b) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) A Statement is laid on the Table of the 
House. 
Statement 
The post of Drugs Controller General of India became available on 1-1-
2002 for filling up on regular basis consequent on the retirement of the incumbent 
of the post. Since the post had been upgraded, the post could not be filled up on 
regular basis as the existing Recruitment Rules (RRs) could not be made operable. 
The revised RRs have since been referred to the Union Public Service Commission 
for approval. However, pending finalisation of RRs, a proposal has been sent to 
Department of Personnel & Training for filling up the post on ad-hoc basis. The 
senior-most officer in the hierarchy is, however, looking after the work of Drugs 
Controller General of India.

Statement 
Diarrhoea and dysentry are water borne diseases and these diseases show 
a seasonal rise of cases during summer. 
Number of cases of acute diarrhoeal diseases detected in the State of 
Rajasthan during 1999-2001 are as follows:  
Year No. of Cases 
1999 1,63,214 
2000 2,39,293 
2001 3,42,001 
Health is primarily a State subject and provision of medical relief for these 
diseases through the primary and community health centres is looked after by 
the State Government. To supplement the efforts of the State Government in 
controlling diseases like diarrhoea and dy sentry. Packets of Oral Rehydration 
Solution are supplied as part of Drug Kits to Sub-centres, Primary Health 
Centres, Community Health Centres and First Referral units under the 
Reproductive Child Health Programme, in order to provide protection against 
dehydration to children. Further, a cen tral sector health programme, i.e. 
National Surveillance Programme for Communicable Diseases (NSPCD), has 
been implemented in phased manner since 1997 in the country. Currently, it is 
in operation in 101 districts including 7 districts of Rajasthan, viz. Alwar, 
Ajmer, Udaipur, Jodhpur, Kota, Sikar and Sirohi. This programme provides 
for early detection and response ot epidemics of communicable diseases, including 
water borne diseases.

Statement-I 
The steps taken by the Government for eradication of dreaded diseases 
such as AIDS, Hepatitis-A/B/C, Cancer, TB, Leprosy etc. 
(i) AIDS 
In order to prevent and control of HIV/AIDS a comprehensive 
Programme is currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
100% centrally sponsored scheme. The main components of the programme 
consist of: 
* Reducing the spread of HIV in groups at high risk by identification of 
target populations and providing peer counselling, condom promotion 
and treatment of sexually transmitted infections. 
* Preventive intervention for the general population by Information, 
Education and Communication (IEC) and awareness campaign, 
provision of voluntary testing and counselling, safe blood transfusion 
services and prevention of occupational exposure. 
* Providing financial assistance for opportunistic infections, home and 
community based care. 
* Strengthening effectiveness and t echnical, managerial, financial 
sustainability of the intervention programmes at National, State and 
Community levels. 
* Promoting collaboration amongst public, private and voluntary 
sectors. 
(ii) Hepatitis-A, B & C 
Hepatitis-A:—It is a water borne disease and is spread through faeco-oral 
route. Vaccine for prevention of Hepatitis-A is not indigenously produced but is 
commercially available in the market. As Hepatitis-A is spread thr ough 
contaminated water, the important prevention and control measures are supply 
of safe drinking water and sanitation in all areas. 
31 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
Hepatitis-B :—It is spread through unsafe sex, unsafe blood transfusion, 
unrafe injections etc. and from mother to child. This is preventable by 
ensuring safe blood transfusion, safe sex, safe injection practices etc. Vaccine for 
Hepatitis-B is available. The following measures have been taken to prevent 
Hepatitis-B:— 
* Central Government Hospital personnel at high risk are being 
immunized against Hepatitis-B. State Governments have also been 
advised to take similiar steps. 
* Guidelines have been issued for mandatory testing of blood in all blood 
banks. 
* Promotion of safe sex under National AIDS Control Programme is 
advocated. 
* Health Awareness Campaigns under National AIDS Control 
Programme are held. 
* Guidelines have been issued to State Health Authorities for use of 
separate sterile syringes and needles for each injection. 
* A Pilot Project to immunize childre n against Hepatitis-B in selected 
Cities/Districts have been launched under National Immunization 
Programme by Deptt. of Family Welfare. 
Hepatitis-C :—It is spread through unsafe sex, unsafe blood transfusion, 
unsafe injections etc.. and from mother  to child. This is preventable by 
ensuring safe b'f 16 transfusion, safe sex, safe injection practices etc. Vaccine 
for Hepati is-C is not available. The following measures have been taken to 
prevent Hepatitis-C:— 
* Mandatory testing of blood in all blood banks. 
* Promotion of safe sex under National AiDS Control Programme is 
advocated. 
* Health Awareness Campaigns under National AIDS Control 
Programme are held. 
* Guidelines have been issued to State Health Authorities for use of 
separate sterile syringes and needles for each injection.

(iii) Cancer 
Under National Cancer Control Programme, there are 20 Regional Cancer 
Centres that are providing comprehensive cancer treatment to the patients and 
conducting research activities. Government of India is providing assistance 
under various schemes of National Cancer Control Programme to Medical 
Colleges/NGOs and State Governments for purchase of Cobalt Unit. Linear 
Accelerator etc. and for conducting aw areness and early detection activities 
on cancer. 
(iv) TB 
To control problem of Tuberculosis National TB Control Programme has 
been in operation since 1962. The programme is integrated with Primary 
Health Care infrastructure and is implemented through a network of 446 Districts 
TB Centres, 330 TB Clinics and about 47,600 beds.The programme was 
reviewed by the Committee of Experts in 1992 and based on the findings of 
Committee. Government of India launched a Revised National TB Control 
Programme (RNTCP) with an aim to cure at least 85% of new sputum 
positive cases and to detect at least 70% of such cases which is being 
implemented in the country in phased manner.

Import of copper wire rods from Sri Lanka 
*537. SHRI S.S. AHLUWALIA: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND 
INDUSTRY be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government's attention has been drawn to the growth of export 
of copper wire rods into India from Sri Lanka; 
(b) the details of import of copper wire rods since 1995-96, year-wise and 
country-wise; 
(c) whether it is a fact that while custom duty of 25 per cent is leviable 
on import of copper wire rods from other countries, only 2 per cent duty is 
levied on import from Sri Lanka; and 
(d) the rationale behind levy of preferential duty on import of copper wire 
rods although Sri Lanka is known to have no copper mines or smelter? 
THE MINISTER OF COMMERCE AND INDUSTRY (SHRI ARUN 
JAITLEY):(a)Yes,Sir. 
(b) The details of import of copper rods and copper wire are given in 
Statement-I and Statement-11 respectively. (See below) 
(c) The basic customs duty on import of copper wire and copper rods from 
other countries is 25%. The import of  these products was permitted at a 
preferential duty of 2.5% from Sri Lanka under the India-Sri Lanka Free Trade 
Agreement (ISLFTA) till 17th March, 2003.  However, with effect from 18th 
March, 2003, these products are being permitted duty free from Sri Lanka. 
(d) The import of copper wire and rods from Sri Lanka is to be allowed at 
preferential duty only subject to fulfillment of the Rules of Origin prescribed 
under the ISLFTA which specify that domestic value addition requirement shall 
be 35% and that the goods must undergo transformation at 4-digit harmonized 
system of Tariff Classification.

HIV Epidemics 
*523. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD : Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware of the reports that serious localized 
HIV epidemics in different parts of the country are affecting millions of people; 
and 
(b) if so, what steps Government have taken in this regard? 
THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE (SHRIMATI 
SUSHMA SWARAJ): (a) and (b) The Na tional AIDS Control Organization, 
Government of India, conducts Nation wide HIV sentinel surveillance every 
year during the period August-October, covering both high-risk groups as well 
as general population. This data is used for both, to monitor the trends of HIV 
infection in different risk groups and to estimate the burden of HIV infections 
in the country in the adult population. The last HIV sentinel surveillance round 
conducted in year 2002 included 384 Sentinel sites located in differet parts of 
the country. These sites include 166 sites in Sexually Transmitted Disease 
(STD) clinics, 13 sites for Intravenous Drug Users (IDUs), 3 sites for Men 
having Sex with Men (MSM), 2 sites for Commercial Sex Workers (CSWs) 
and 200 sites located in antenatal clinics representing general population. Based 
on the consistent high prevalence in high-risk groups as well as among preg-
nant women attending antenatal clinics, 49 districts have been identified as high 
prevalence districts. This indicates that there is no uniform spread of HIV 
infection, and localized high prevalence is  occurring in different parts of the 
country. The estimated number of HIV infections in the country is about 4 
million. 
In order to prevent and control the spread of HIV/AIDS in India, Gov-
ernment of India has launched a comprehensive National AIDS Control 
Programme, currently under implementation throughout the country as a 
centrally sponsored scheme with the following components: 
54 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
o    Preventive interventions for high risk population through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including - 
counseling and behaviour change communication. 
o Preventive interventions for the general population through grammes 
for blood safety, voluntary counseling and testing services, 
prevention of parent to child transmission of HIV, Information 
Education and Communication (IEC) & awareness building among 
adolescents and sensitization for the AIDS Vaccine Initiative. 
o Provision of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
o  Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public-prival   . nerships. 
o Building technical and managerial capacities for programme 
implementation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and 
Evaluation, Technical resource gr oups, operational research and 
Programme management.

3870. SHRI B. P. SINGHAL: Will the Minister of COMMERCE AND

standards and thus lower the credibility of Indian ISO certifications; 
(d) whether there are any guidelines i ssued by the International Ac-
creditation Forum (IAF) prohibiting oper ations of certification as well as 
consulting services under the same umbrella; and 
(e) if so, the action Government have taken to detect the violation of the 
above guidelines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF COMMERCE 
AND INDUSTRY (SHRI CHENMAMANENI VIDYA SAGAR RAO): (a) 
Yes, Sir. Government are aware of th e several Franchisees of the Foreign

(b) As per information available with Quality Council of India (QCI), an 
autonomous body under the Department of IPP, responsible for accredition of

and how the transactions of the local franchisee are audited by their parent

(c) and (d) While in some cases the dilution of norms of ISO certification 
and quality standards may be possible, there are specific IAF guidance 
document to the ISO/IEC Guide 62 and 66 that clearly describe the non-
permissible relationship between certification and consulting services. 
(e) The responsibility of monitoring the certification and consultancy 
relationship is the direct responsibility of the respective accreditation council. 
In case any of the issues related to malpractices in the certification process

of the different countries of the world as members. The Multilateral 
Arrangement (MLA) of mutual recognition governs the process of mutual 
recognition of the certifi cates accredited by the accreditation body members 
of IAF. 
Through the membership of IAF, NABCB has brought to the notice of IAF 
the deteriorating standards of certification having accreditation from the foreign 
countries. Based on the efforts of NABCB : IAF is working for specific 
guidance document on the cross-frontie r accreditation, which will help of 
improving the standards of the certification in India.

Times of India dated 7 April 2003. This news item points out that the developing 
countries are getting increasingly disenchanted with the current negotiations 
under the Doha Work Programme and that  lack of progress in fulfilling the 
promises made at Doha would make it difficult to achieve progress at Cancun.

Ministers at Doha on the three issu es of importance to the developing 
countries namely TRIPS and Public  Health, Special and Differential 
Treatment; and the Implementation-related issues and concerns could not be 
adhered to India and other developing countries have strongly voiced their 
concerns in the WTO on the slow progress of the negotiations in these areas. 
As pointed out by India at the last meeting of the WTO Trade 
Negotiations Committee (TNC) held in Geneva earlier this month, success at

3906. SHRIABANI ROY: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY 
WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether the National Institute of Communicable Diseases has failed 
to provide timely diagnostic investigations during mysterious outbreaks; 
(b) if so, whether Government have assessed the cause of failure of NICD 
during mysterious outbreaks; 
(c) if so, the details thereof; 
(d) whether Government propose to review the functioning of NICD and 
to make it effective; and 
(e) if so, the details thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (e) National Institute of Com-
municable Diseases (NICD) investigates disease outbreaks in different parts of 
the country round the year on the request of State Health Authorities or as per 
epidemiological requirement. In most situations, the methods are well 
established and containment measures are advocated to the concerned State 
Government authorities. However, in some situations when the disease 
presentation is complex, in-depth advanced laboratory investigations are often 
required which is time consuming. In reported disease outbreaks involving new 
emerging pathogens of communicable diseases or due to non-communicable 
agents, NICD seeks support from other national and international agencies to 
diagnose and control the outbreaks, if required. The preliminary reports 
submitted by NICD after each investigation are timely and based on the 
clinico-epidemio-logical and field observations, and diagnosed to the extent of 
taking immediate control measures which are communicated to the concerned 
State Governments immediately. 
As per data available, NICD has responded immediately by investigating a 
total of 75 outbreaks or conducting health status assessments during 1997-
2001 all over the country relating to different diseases on the request of 
various State Governments. During the year 2002 a total of 14 outbreaks have 
been investigated by NICD. As the Institute is performing its duties well, there 
is no proposal to review its functioning. However, certain plan schemes are 
envisaged during the Tenth Plan to further strengthen the activities of the 
Institute.

3923. SHRI NANDI YELLAIAH: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government are aware that a German research report has claimed 
that potato chips and french fry contain acrylmide acid which can cause cancer in 
foetus and newly bom babies through mothermilk; 
(b) if so, whether Government propose to conduct a research in this regard 
to find the truth and direct the companies manufacturing potato chips and 
french fry to print warning on packets of these eatables for pregnant women 
and lactating mothers; and 
(c) if not, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (c) According to Indian Council of 
Medical Research (ICMR) acrylmide has been found in a range of cooked and 
heat-processed foods. In Humans, studies of workers exposed to acrylmide 
through air and contact with their skin reported no evidence of cancer, though 
prolonged exposure to acrylmide is reported to cause a range of tumors in 
animals (rats and mice). World Health Organisation (WHO) documents also 
indicate that a clear picture of the nature and the level of risk from acrylmide 
does not exist.

New polio cases 
3927.  SHRIPRASANTACHATTERJEE: 
SHRIMATI CHANDRA KALA PANDEY: 
Will the Minister of HEALTH AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that 83 per cen t of all new polio cases are found 
in our country; and 
(b) the special steps Government propose  to take to combat the deadly 
disease? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Yes, Sir. During 2002, India re-
ported 83 per cent of all new cases reported globally. 
(b) The pulse polio immunization is being intensified during 2003-04 as 
against 2002-03. As against two national immunization rounds and two sub-
national immunization rounds during 2002-03, the 2003-04 strategy 
recommended by Indian Advisory Expert Group comprises of four sub-
national immunization rounds in 10 high-risk States during April 03 (already 
conducted), June 03, September 03 and November 03 and two national rounds 
during January and February, 04. 
Following special measures have been taken with special reference to the 
States where large number of polio cases have been detected. 
(i) In order to improve the detecti on and vaccination of missed children, 
the house-to-house vaccination teams in Uttar Pradesh (which 
reported about 78 per cent of total cases in the country during 2002), 
have been strengthened with the addition of a third member from 
within the local community. 
(ii) The community mobilisers have been engaged for improving the 
implementation of the programme in resistant areas. 
(iii) The house-to-house vaccination of missed children is being done for 
five days after the booth day as against two day in other parts of the 
country. 
(iv) Additional Information, Education and Communication (IEC) ac-
tivities are being conducted. 
(v) The implementation of the programme is being closely monitored at 
the apex political and bureaucratic levels both in the Government of 
India as also in the States. 
121 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
(vi) Local influencers/social and religious leaders are being involved for 
advocacy and ensuring greater participation of the people in the 
programme. 
(vii) One surveillance Medical Officer has been posted in each districts in 
order to help the States in ensuring better monitoring and 
supervision.

FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Infection is a major cause of 
deaths in the neo-natal period, i.e. the first month of life, indeed throughout the 
first year of life. 
(b) The proportion of babies delivered at the Government health care 
facilities is steadily improving and the rates vary considerably in different 
parts of India. Most of those not delivered at Government health facilities are 
attended by local birth attendants who have been trained by the Government 
and provided a safe delivery kit. 
(c) Vigorous efforts by the Government are underway to ensure safe 
delivery and optimal new born care throughout the country as follows:— 
 
(1) Improvement in physical infrastruct ure at Primary Health Centres 
and first level referral hospitals were made under the RCH 
Programme. 
(2) Extensive In-service training for physicians, ANMs and Dais with 
provision of appropriate tools provided throughout the country. 
(3) Measures were taken to improve neo-natal care at first level referral 
hospitals under a special programme coordinated by National 
Neonatology Forum. Appropriate Neo-na^al Care equipment provided 
in the districts where training was completed. 
(4) The Indian Council of Medical Research has initiated a project on Home 
Based Management of Young Infants (0-60 days) in rural areas of fiye 
States (Bihar, Orissa, Uttar Pradesh, Maharashtra and Rajasthan) for 
reduction of neo-natal mortality.

FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that India has the largest number of AIDS and TB 
infections in the region; 
(b) if so, the number of patients, State-wise; and 
(c) the plans of Government to control these diseases? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) Yes, Sir. 
(b) A Statement - I indicating St ate-wise reported number of 
cumulative AIDS cases as on 31st Ma rch, 2003 is annexed. (See below):

2002 is also annexed (See below). 
(c) The following Steps have been taken by the Government to con 
trol these diseases, (i) AIDS: In orde r to prevent and control of HIV/AIDS 
in India, Government of India has launched a comprehensive National 
AIDS Control Programme, is currently under implementation throughout 
the country as a Centrally sponsored scheme with the following 
components:— 
• QPreventive interventions for high risk populations through targeted 
interventions adopting a multi-pronged strategy including peer 
counselling and behaviour change communication. 
• Preventive intervention for the general population through 
programmes for blood safety, voluntary counselling and testing 
services, Prevention of parent to child transmission of HIV, 
information education and communication (IEC) and awareness 
building among adolescents and se nsitization for the AIDS Vaccine 
Initiative. 
• Providing of low cost care and support services by providing 
community care services, treatment of opportunistic infections and 
prevention of occupational exposure. 
• Collaborative efforts to promote inter-sectoral programme activities 
including workplace interventions and public-private partnership.

• Building technical and managerial  capacities for programme imple-
mentation through Surveillance, Training, Monitoring and Evaluation, 
Technical Resource Groups, Opera tional research and Programme 
management. 
(ii) TB: National TB Control Programme has been in operation since 1962 
in the entire country as a Centrally sponsored programme. Under the 
programme all diagnostic and treatment facilities including supply of 
anti TB drugs for full course of tr eatment are provided to all TB 
patients free of cost. To achieve a cure rate of 85% of new sputum 
positive cases and to detect at least 70% of such cases revised National 
TB Control Programme (RNTCP) widely known as DOTS, which is a 
WHO recommended strategy, is being implemented in the country in a 
phased manner. More than 600 million population has already been 
covered under the strategy. It is envisaged to cover 850 million 
population by 2004 and the entire country by 2005. The Project 
Districts have reported a cure rate of more than 80% which means more 
than 8 out of every 10 patients diagnosed and put on treatment under 
the revised strategy are successfully treated. To increase accessibility to 
the TB care facilities, emphasis is laid on involvement of NGOs, 
Private Practitioners and Medical Colleges in the revised strategy. To 
create mass awareness that TB is fully curable and that all diagnostic 
and treatment facilities including supply of anti TB drugs for full course 
of treatment are provided free of cost to all TB patients under the 
Programme, IEC activities are undertaken at all levels.

Report on banned medicines 
3932. PROF. M. SA NKARALINGAM: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that Delhi High Court recently asked for a report 
on medicines banned World-wide; 
(b) the complete details thereof; 
(c) whether it is also a fact that the banned medicines which are prohibited 
for children below three years are being used in the country; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof and if not, the reasons therefor?   . 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) No, Sir. The Hon'ble High 
Court of Delhi has, however, asked for a report on the safety and approval of 
the drug Nimesulide and its formulations in.the matter of a PIL filed by Social 
Jurist Vs. Govt, of India. A detailed examination has been undertaken by an 
expert committee (Sub-Committee) of Drug Technical Advisory Board to 
deliberate on the issue concerning the safety of Nimesulide, including its use 
in children. More than 20 expert paediatricians across the country and the 
Indian Academy of Paediatrics (IAP) were consulted. Majority of experts have 
confirmed the reliability of Nimesulide and no serious adverse reaction in 
children have been reported in the country. The drug has not been prohibited 
in any of the major countries of the world either for adult use orpaediatric use. 
Preventive action against SARS 
3933. SHRI RAJKUMAR DHOOT: Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased, to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that pneumonia (SARS) scare failed to goad 
Government to take prompt preventive action in India; 
(b) whether Government are aware that TV media coverage on 4th April, 
2003 has shown that the much hyped arrangements for checking of passengers 
arriving from Hong Kong, Singapore, Malaysia, etc. at the airports were not 
seen and that the passengers were cleared without adequate safeguards; 
(c) the steps taken to make adequate arrangements and whether situation 
has improved now; and 
130 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(d) if so, the details thereof and the outcome thereof? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) to (d) No, Sir. Following reports of 
outbreak of Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS) in some countries 
Government of India has taken adequate steps to prevent entry of the disease in to 
the country and to isolate and treat a case if reported. The steps include screening of 
all persons disembarking in India for symptoms of suspect/probable SARS cases. For 
this purpose a proforma has been prepared by the Ministry of Health and Family 
Welfare and handed over to concerned authorities. The health care facilities at 
International Airports and Ports have been strengthened by deploying 
additional doctors and evolving a standard operating protocol. The hearth staff is 
monitoring passengers disembarking in India to report any suspected case 
and to take further appropriate action. 
Hospitals have been identified w ith isolation facilities where the 
passengers with SARS like symptoms would be immediately shifted for 
further management. 
Prevalence of spurious drugs in the Market 
3934. SHRI MANOJ BHATTACHARYA: Will the Minister of HEALTH 
AND FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether Government with the assi stance of an N.G.O. namely the 
Delhi Society for the Promotion of  Rational Use of Drugs (DSPRUD) has 
undertaken an extensive survey of the market in Delhi, Haryana, M.P. and 
U.P. to gauge the prevalence of spurious drugs; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether the task force constituted to undertake the work consists of 
qualified pharmacists to help it in its work; 
(d) by when, the report is likely to finalized and published; and 
(t) what steps are in the meanwhile being taken to curb the sale of 
spurious drugs in the market which has assumed alarming proportions? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a ) to (d) The Delhi Society forthe 
Promotion of Rational Use of Drugs (DSPRUD)—a non-governmental 
organization has informed that they would be conducting a survey as a 
131 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
pilot study in Delhi State only to gauge the extent of spurious drugs in the 
market. The task force includes qualified pharmacists. Their report is likely to 
be finalized and published by them around January, 2004. 
(e) Since manufacture and sale of spurious drugs is mainly a clandestine 
activity indulge in by anti social persons, steps are taken from time to time by 
enforcement authorities of the States to detect and unearth spurious/fake 
drugs in the inter-state commerce. Government of India has taken the 
following steps:— 
The Drugs Controller General (India) has advised the state drugs 
controllers to take the following meas ures for curbing the incidence of 
spurious drugs:— 
(i) Constitution/reactivation of the State Drug Advisory Committee in 
which various state and industry associations as well consumer 
associations would find representation. 
(ii) Establishment of separate in telligence-cum-legal machinery with 
police assistance. Training should be provided to selected officials of 
Drugs Control Administration in the modalities of intelligence 
work, prosecution etc. in respect of spurious/counterfeit drugs. 
(iii) To ensure speedy analysis of drug samples by establishing own state 
level drug testing facilities. 
(iv) State Drugs Control Authorities should be cautious while approving 
licenses for drug products to ensure that "look-alike" products are 
not encouraged. 
(v) To develop efficient communication facilitates and recall procedures. 
(vi)    Surveillance of suspected dealers. 
(vii)    Engaging experienced counsel for fighting spurious drug cases. 
(viii) Cooperation of pharmaceutical industry by regular interaction with 
them. 
(ix) Collection of survey samples under National Survey Quality 
Evaluation of Drugs (NSQED) Programme. 
• The Union Minister of Health & Family Welfare had written on Oct. 8, 
2002 to all the Chief Ministers seeking their personal 
132 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
intervention to ensure that adequate measures are taken in each 
State to deal with this problem. Union Minister of Health & Family 
Welfare also convened a meeting of the Health Ministers and 
senior officials of 13 major States of the country on 12.11.2002 to 
discuss measures to ensure consorted action required to check 
movement of spurious drugs in the country and to involve all 
stakeholders, including pharma industry, to curb the menace of 
manufacture and marketing of spurious/ fake medicines. 
Union Ministry of Health & Family Welfare constituted a Com-
mittee underthe chairmanship of DGHS to examine the extent of 
problem and suggest remedial measures. Committee report has been 
submitted along with its recommendation in July 2002. A copy of 
the report of the Committee constituted by the Government of India 
to examine the issues concerning availability of spurious drugs in 
the market and measures recommended thereof have been sent to all 
the State Drugs Controllers for their implementation. 
• Government of India has set up an expert committee on January 
27,2003 underthe Chairmanship of DR. R.A. Mashelkar, DG, 
CSIR and Secretary to Govt, of India to look into various issues 
related to drugs control administration including the matter of 
effectively tackling the problem of spurious drugs. 
• Central Government have taken steps to augment the drugs testing 
facilities of State laboratories. Strengthening information system 
through computer networking is also under implementation.

142

(b) Government of India, Department of Family Welfare has various 
schemes to bring down the Infant Mortality Rate. The recent initiative, 
Reproductive and Child Health (RCH) Programme launching in 1997, is under 
implementation in all States. Under this, immunisation against six vaccine 
preventable diseases, facilities for appropriate management of acute 
respiratory infections, Oral Rehydration Therapy (ORT) for management of 
diarrhoeal diseases and essential new born care services are provided. Promotion 
of exclusive breastfeeding and appropriate complementary feeding practices and 
prophylaxis againt Vitamin-A and iron deficiencies are also provided to improve

Child Development Services, which looks after the nutritional requirements of

World Bank assistance under R&CH Programme 
3940. MS. PRAMILA BOHIDAR : Will the Minister of HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE be pleased to state: 
(a) whether World Bank has provided financial assistance under 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme in the country; 
(b) if so, the details thereof; 
(c) whether population growth has been brought under control on 
account of this programme; and 
(d) if so, the details thereof ? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF HEALTH AND 
FAMILY WELFARE (SHRI A. RAJA): (a) and (b) Yes, Sir. The World Bank has 
provided external assistance of Rs. 800.59 crores till 31.3.2003 for 
 145 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
he Reproductive and Child Health Programme under World Bank ITF Credit 
No. 018-IN. In addition, the World Bank has also provided assistance of Rs. 
386.97 crores under IDA Credit No. 3340 for Immunization Strengthening 
Project which is also being implemented as a part of the overall RCH 
Programme. 
(c) and (d) Population growth is influenced by a variety of factors 
including many not directly related to provision of health services. The 
Reproductive and Child Health Programme indirectly influences the population 
growth by assuring the survival of children and mothers, and thereby reducing the 
level of wanted fertility. 
The annual population growth rate has declined from 1.83% in 1997, *he 
year in which RCH Programme was launched,to 1.70% (provisional) in 2001, 
whereas the crude birth rate has, during the same period, de-dined from 27.2% 
to 25.4% (provisional), as per results of Sample Reg-stration Surveys released 
by Registrar General of India.

provide anti-malaria drugs for early treatment through health facilities and 
community volunteers and integrated vector control which include indoor 
residual spray in the high risk poGkets in rural areas, laravicides in urban areas, 
use of insecticide treated bednets, larvivorous fish and environmental measures.

Central Sector and Centrally Sponsored Schemes 
4006. SHRIMATIPREMACARIAPPA: 
SHRIMOTILALVORA: 
Will the Minister of URB AN DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY 
ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) the details of different Central Sector schemes and Centrally 
Sponsored Schemes being implemented by his Ministry; 
(b) the financial institutions involved in above said schemes; and 
(c) the contribution of these financial institutions under the existing 
guidelines? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) to (c) The detail s of Central Sector schemes and 
Centrally Sponsored schemes being implemented by this Ministry and the 
contribution of the financial institutions under the existing guidelines of the 
schemes is as under:— 
1. Integrated Development of Small and Medium Towns (IDSMT)— The 
main objective of the scheme is to improve infrastructural facilities 
and help in the creation of durable assets in Small and Medium 
Towns. As per the guidelines, 20-40% of the project cost can be 
obtained from financial institutions or other sources. While there is a 
limit on Central assistance depending on the size of the town, there 
is no ceiling on the amounts that could be made available from the 
State Governments/Local bodi es from out of their own 
resources/Institutional financing Agencies. 
201 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
2. Infrastructural Develqpment in Mega Cities—The funds under the 
scheme flow from the Central and State Governments directly to the 
nodal agencies designated by the State Governments for development 
of infrastructure in the Cities of Mumbai, Kolkata, Hyderabad, 
Chennai and Bangalore. The sharing between the Central Government 
and State Government is 25% : 25%. The balance 50% is required to 
be mobilised by the nodal agencies/implementing agencies from 
Financial Institutions. 
3. Accelerated Urban Water Supply Programme (AUWSP)—The 
scheme has the objective of solving the drinking water problems in 
towns having population of less than 20,000 as per 1991 census. The 
scheme is funded on grant basis, by the Central Government 50% and 
State Government 50% including 5% beneficiary/town contribution. 
In case of Union Territories, 100% financing is available from the 
Central Share. No Institutional Finance is involved in the scheme. 
4. Low Cost Sanitation for Liberation of Scavengers (LCS)—The 
objective of the scheme is to convert dry units into twin pit-pour flush 
units and to construct new units where no facility is available for 
improving the sanitation conditions and to liberate scavengers. Under the 
scheme, loan and subsidy is extended simultaneously by Housing & 
Urban Development Corporation Ltd. (HUDCO), a techno-financial 
Public Sector Undertaking (PSU) under this Ministry, after the 
sanction of the scheme for the construction upto the sub-structure. For 
this purpose, Centra! subsidy is routed through HUDCO. The loan and 
subsidy portion is based on the income of the beneficiaries with the 
objective to provide subsidies to lower income groups only. 
5. Swarna Jayanti Shahari Rojgar Yojana (SJSRY)— The Scheme 
provides assistance to individual urban poor beneficiaries or groups of 
urban poor women for setting of gainful self employment ventures. 
Training is also given to the beneficiaries and other persons associated 
with the programme for upgradation and acquisition of vocational and 
entrepreneurial skills. Under the Urban Self Employment Programme 
(USEP) component of the SJSRY scheme subsidy is provided at the 
rate of 15% of the project cost subject to a ceiling of Rs. 7500/-per 
beneficiary to set up Micro Enterprises. Each beneficiary is 
202 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
required to contribute 5% of the project cost as margin money in cash. 
Loan (inclusive of subsidy) upto 95% of the project cost can be 
sanctioned as composite loans by banks. 
For Development of Women and Children in Urban Areas (DWCUA) 
component of USEP, DWCUA group society is entitled to a subsidy of Rs. 
1,25,000/- or 50% of the cost of project whichever is less. 
6. Shelter and Sanitation Ffacilitie s for the Ffootpath Dwellers in 
Urban Areas (Night Shelter Scheme) —Fund under the scheme is 
provided for construction of composite Night Shelters with 
Community toilets and baths for urban shelterless. The scheme is 
being implemented through HUDCO which provides loan to the 
implementing agencies to meet the balance cost of the project after 
the release of Central Subsidy. The Central Subsidy is also 
channelised through HUDCO. 
7. National Network of Building Centres—Fund were provided under 
the scheme for setting up Building Centres. The Building Centres 
impart training to the artisans, demonstration of various cost effective 
building technologies, energy efficient and environment friendly 
building components and technology transfer from lab to land. This 
scheme was also being implemented through HUDCO. However, the 
scheme has since been discontinued in the Tenth Five Year Plan. A 
proposal for revival of the scheme has been taken up with the 
Planning Commission. 
8. Valmiki Ambedkar Awas Yojana (Vambay)—The Scheme has the 
primary objective to facilitate the construction and upgradation of the 
dwelling units for the slum dwellers and to provide health and 
enabling urban environment through community toilets. The 
Governemnt of India subsidy is of 50%, the balance 50% is to be 
arranged by the State Government. The State's share may consist of 
funds from any sources in the form of subsidy or loan from HUDCO 
or any other agency. Government of India subsidy is released after the 
State's matching share of 50% has been released. The subsidy is 
released through HUDCO. 
9. Urban Mapping Scheme —The scheme envisage use of modem 
technique of aerial photography and remote sensing for preparation 
and updating of existing base maps by adopting computerbases 
Geographic Information System (GIS) and the 
203 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
techniques of remote sensing for urban planning and development. The 
scheme is funded 100% by Central Government and executed through 
Town and Country Planning Organisation (TCPO). No Financial 
Institution is involved in the scheme. 
10. Urban Transport Planning—The Grant Assistance is provided to 
State Governments under the scheme for conducting feasibility studies 
and preparation of detailed Project Reports in the Urban Transport 
Sector. No Financial Institution is involved in the scheme. 
11. Provision of Infrastructural Facilities in Displaced Persons Urban 
Colonies in West Bengal—The funds under the scheme is provided for 
provision of water supply, drainage, roads and pathways, sanitation 
and other items, in the refugee colonies. The funds are directly released 
to the Government of West Bengal. No financial Institution is involved 
in the scheme. 
12. (a)    Public Health Engineering Training Programme (PHE 
Training) 
(b) Research and Development (R&D) 
(c) Monitoring and Management Information System (MIS) 
PHE Training programme caters to the training needs of various Water Supply 
and Sanitation Departments in the field of Public Health Engineering. Under 
Research and Development, the Ministry sponsors applied research and 
development projects to various research and academic institutions in the 
field of water supply sanitation and solid waste management. Under 
Monitoring and Management Information System, the Ministry is 
contemplating to get the Centrally sponsored schemes such as AUWSP and 
LCS evaluated through independent agencies. 
No Institutional Finance is involved in these scheme. 
Contaminated Water Supply in Delhi 
4007. SHRI GHULAM NABI AZAD : Will the Minister of URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION be pleased to state: 
(a) whether it is a fact that scant respect for quality checks and 
ineffective purification methods result in contaminated water supply in Delhi; 
204 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
(b) if so, whether the quality of drinking water in Delhi is steadily 
declining; 
(c) if so, the reasons therefor; 
(d) whether Government are aware that the entire rural belt of Delhi is being 
supplied with untreated ground water; and 
(e) if so, the reasons therefor? 
THE MINISTER OF STATE IN THE MINISTRY OF URBAN 
DEVELOPMENT AND POVERTY ALLEVIATION (SHRI PON 
RADHAKRISHNAN): (a) to (c) The Delhi Jal Board (DJB) has informed that 
effective purification methods are adopted by DJB so that the water qua lity 
conforms to the standards laid down by Central Public Health and Environmental 
Engineering Organisation (CPHEEO) of Ministry of Urban Development & 
Poverty Alleviation and the Bureau of Indian Standards (IS: 10500). Regular 
surveillance of quality of water is done by lifting the water samples right from 
raw water intake point to the consumer's end and testing the same for various 
parameters like chlorine content, t oxic metals, pesticides etc. The water 
supplied by Delhi Jal Board is safe, wholesome and potable. 
(d) and (e) DJB has informed that potable ground water which is only 13.5% 
of total water supply, is duly treated with chlorine and supplied in Delhi including 
rural belt. However, in a few villages situated at the periphery where ground water 
is not portable, drinking water is suplied through water tankers.

education. Both the central and Stat e Governments have introduced a

particular the 'San/a Shiksha Abhiyan' or 'Education for' All' compaign

that two hundred million students in the age group of 14 to I6yrs have enrolled

is the sum and substance of the repor t. It means that though a number of 
students join schools, many of them drop out. there are a number of schemes 
introduced by the Central and State Governments. In Andhra Pradesh 
Schemes like Malli Badiki (Back to school), Chaduvual Panduga (Festival of 
education) were launched. A Mid day Meal scheme has Jalso been introduced 
with the assistance of the Central Government, through this scheme the 
Andhra Padesh Goernment is able to provide food to lakhs of students 
everyday. For this programme the State Government is spending Rs.230 
crores more, in addition to the funds a llocated by the Centre for the purchase

by the Mother's associations/societies set up

PROF. M. SANKARALINGAM (Tamil Nadu ): Mr. Vice Chairman, Sir, 
the development of a country depends u pon the talent, intellectual skill and 
the ability of its people to rise to a le vel, which a country expects from its 
people. The skilled technological efficiency of our people; their scientific 
advancement, which is comparable with that of the world standard, and their 
devotion to the cause of our country will, certainly, take us on a par with 
developed countries of the world. Each and every person, born in our country, 
should be so moulded as to reach this  level of expectation. In brief, the 
Human Resource Development Ministry must aim to achieve this end. 
278 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
We are committed to provide free and compulsory primary education 
to all our children. It is more than half-a century since we achieved our 
Independence; still we have not been able to achieve any commensurate 
progress in thij vital field. We are committed to provide free and compulsory 
elementary education to all the children between the age group of 6 to 14 
years. Primary education should be impa rted in the Government Institutions, 
and they should have a uniform syllabus throughout the country. The State 
Governments and the Central Government should evolve a joint policy; since 
Education is in the Concurrent List, both should bear the burden equally, and 
joint monitoring should be done periodically. Up to the eighth standard, 
mother tongue should be the medium of  instruction, and any other regional 
language, or, even English, should be taught only as a special subject. Now, 
the private institutions have developed a sort of mania for English as a 
medium of instruction. This Is not a healthy sign. This really neglects the rural 
poor people, who can never compete with  the rich urban students. Learning 
subjects through a foreign language is Just like a married couple, who are 
living separately, a thousand miles apart, leading their family life over phone. 
At high school and higher secondary levels, that is, from g"' to 12" 
standards, at present, it is oriented towa rds university education. The need of 
the present-day society is a comprehens ive and integrated plan for improving 
the quality of school education. Vocational  subjects should find a place in the 
curriculum. Two or three allied subjects like stenography, accountancy, 
computer application and other technical subjects should be included in the 
syllabus. Commercial subjects like accountancy, auditing, etc. should also be 
taught. For all these, practical trai ning should also be given. Having 
infrastructural facilities must be the pr econdition for starting such schools. Let 
the NCERT be given a free hand to evol ve a useful integrated system for 
school education. The NCERT has experimental, research and developmental 
wings at its command. At this stage, every year, nearly 60,000 software 
engineers and Diploma holders are produced in our country, of which 25,000 
accounts from Tamil Nadu. To create employment opportunities, the then 
Tamil Nadu Government planned for tidal parks at Chennai and the same was 
inaugurated by our hon. Prime Minister  in the year 2000. The then Chief 
Minister announced at the inaugural fu nction itself, " Tidal phase II and III are 
planned" but that has not materialised till now. I request the Central 
Government to see that the innovative scheme is implemented. The Scheme 
of the then Tamil Nadu Government to im part computer education in all high 
schools has to be 
279 

RAJYA SABHA [28 April, 2003] 
completed.    To  start  with,  the  then  Government  started  hundred  high 
schools. It has to be completed now. 
Moreover, university is regarded as a temple of devotion to the 
advancement of higher learning. Since t he days of our ancient universities of 
Nalanda, Taxila and Vikramshila, our country has undergone a lot of changes; 
therefore, the style of ed ucation has also to be changed. We have raised the 
number of universities, that is, from 19 at the time of Independence in 1947 to 
219 in 1997, in a period of 50 years. The quality of higher education has to be 
preserved at any cost. In this connection , I wish to bring to  the notice of the 
Government the answer given by the hon. Minister for Human Resource 
Development on 7.8.2001 to a Starred Question No. 221 on the floor of the 
Lok Sabha, and I quote, "The Universi ty Grants Commission has identified 19 
fake universities functioning in the country." See what kind of havoc they have 
played with our youngsters.    Such kind of criminal activities should be dealt 
with severely. 
In recent years, India seems to be undergoing a revolutionary 
change in higher education. If the take-o ff is in the right direction, we can 
welcome the same, but, unfortunately, the take-off is in the wrong direction. 
Thousands of spurious colleges and dozens  of spurious universities, without 
minimum infrastructure and resources, have sprung up like mushrooms, 
despite the existence of  monitoring mech anisms like the U.G.C., AICTE, the 
task force of the Government and all powe rful committees of the Universities. 
These are responsible for maintaining education standards. Some of the 
private technical colleges are minting mo ney and they are run as an industry 
of profit. By all means, this should be put an end to by the State and the 
Central Governments, with full c oordination and understanding. All the 
engineering colleges and other technical colleges should have industries and 
factories of their own. The courses shoul d be limited to such a level that the 
students studying there should be trained in their factories, to be trained in 
such a way that the outgoing students must be competent to work in factories, 
or, start their own industries, instead of seeking white-collar jobs. The existing 
private engineering colleges be advised to  start industries to cope up with the 
norms prescribed. After two years of theoretical classes, all the students 
should be given apprentice training for tw o or three years in their industries 
itself. 
The Industrial Revolution of the I8 lh Century in England created a 
great demand for skilled engineers.   (Time-bell)   Sir, I will just finish.   The 
280 

[28 April, 2003] RAJYA SABHA 
engineering colleges in England started courses with less theoretical syllabus, 
and more practical training and apprenticeship in a factory was a part of the 
course. It was highly successful to meet the situation in the 18* Century. This 
kind of education has to be adopted with  regard to the technical education in 
our country also. Recently, the Railway Ministry has adopted a system of 
informal education for their mechanical engineers in their cadre. Some 
ordnance factories have also adopted similar informal education for their staff. 
Our graduates are more theoretical  than practical. That is why 
entrepreneurship scheme has failed miserably. They need practical training, 
which shapes and builds their confidence necessary for success. 
The National Policy on Education was evolved in May, 1986. After a 
comprehensive appraisal of the then existing scenario of education, this was 
published in about 14 languages for a national debate. The National Policy on 
Education was unanimously passed by Parliament. 
Presently, the Ministry of Human Resource Development is under 
the able guidance and leadership of our great scholar and scientist, Dr. Murli 
Manohar Joshi. Now,- he has to lead the country in this direction, which I 
mentioned above. The challenge before us is to plan for education towards 
human resource development from a holistic perspective for nation building in 
our pluralistic secular society. Let all of  us contribute our might for this noble 
cause under the leadership of eminent scholar, Dr. Murli Manohar Joshi. 
With these words, Sir, I conclude.   Thank you.
